claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, RNA polymerase II (Pol II) selects transcription start sites (TSSs) by a unidirectional scanning process.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, RNA polymerase II (Pol II) selects transcription start sites (TSSs) by a unidirectional scanning process.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work establishing scanning mechanisms.

claim: During scanning, a preinitiation complex (PIC) assembled at an upstream core promoter initiates at select positions within a window ~40–120 bp downstream.
source: During scanning, a preinitiation complex (PIC) assembled at an upstream core promoter initiates at select positions within a window ~40–120 bp downstream.
evidence: This statement describes the scanning window distance, which is supported by prior literature and data in the manuscript.

claim: Ssl2, the yeast homolog of XPB, is an essential and conserved subunit of the general transcription factor (GTF) TFIIH.
source: Ssl2, the yeast homolog of XPB and an essential and conserved subunit of the general transcription factor (GTF) TFIIH
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ssl2/XPB being part of TFIIH.

claim: Ssl2 drives scanning through its DNA-dependent ATPase activity.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that Ssl2, the yeast homolog of XPB and an essential and conserved subunit of the general transcription factor (GTF) TFIIH, drives scanning through its DNA-dependent ATPase activity
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence cited in the manuscript.

claim: Novel ssl2 alleles confer either upstream or downstream TSS shifts at the model promoter ADH1 and genome-wide.
source: These ssl2 alleles, many of which alter residues conserved from yeast to human, confer either upstream or downstream TSS shifts at the model promoter ADH1 and genome-wide.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Tested ssl2 alleles alter TSS selection by increasing or narrowing the distribution of TSSs used at individual promoters.
source: Specifically, tested ssl2 alleles alter TSS selection by increasing or narrowing the distribution of TSSs used at individual promoters.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TSS-seq data and quantification shown in figures.

claim: Genetic interactions of ssl2 alleles with other initiation factors are consistent with ssl2 allele classes functioning through increasing or decreasing scanning processivity but not necessarily scanning rate.
source: Genetic interactions of ssl2 alleles with other initiation factors are consistent with ssl2 allele classes functioning through increasing or decreasing scanning processivity but not necessarily scanning rate.
evidence: This interpretation is based on genetic interaction data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The outcome of promoter scanning is determined by two functional networks: one being Pol II activity and factors that modulate it to determine initiation efficiency within a scanning window, and the second being Ssl2/TFIIH and factors that modulate scanning processivity to determine the width of the scanning window.
source: We propose that the outcome of promoter scanning is determined by two functional networks, the first being Pol II activity and factors that modulate it to determine initiation efficiency within a scanning window, and the second being Ssl2/TFIIH and factors that modulate scanning processivity to determine the width of the scanning widow.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the integration of all experimental findings in the study.

claim: Transcription of eukaryotic protein-coding genes is carried out by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) in three sequential steps: initiation, elongation, and termination.
source: Transcription of eukaryotic protein-coding genes is carried out by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) in three sequential steps: initiation, elongation, and termination (Roeder, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Accurate initiation requires minimally the assistance of five general transcription factors (GTFs) TFIIB, TFIID, TFIIE, TFIIF, and TFIIH, which together with Pol II, comprise the basal transcription machinery.
source: Accurate initiation requires minimally the assistance of five general transcription factors (GTFs) TFIIB, TFIID, TFIIE, TFIIF, and TFIIH, which together with Pol II, comprise the basal transcription machinery.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the transcription machinery.

claim: Initial promoter melting appears to occur stereotypically ~20–25 nt downstream of promoter elements such as the TATA box across eukaryotes.
source: Initial promoter melting appears to occur stereotypically ~20–25 nt downstream of promoter elements such as the TATA box across eukaryotes, though most promoters lack a TATA box or other strong sequence signature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about promoter melting positions.

claim: Differences in 5' UTR can alter transcript properties such as translation efficiency or transcript stability through differences in sequence or RNA secondary structure.
source: Differences in 5' UTR can alter transcript properties such as translation efficiency or transcript stability through differences in sequence or RNA secondary structure (Arribere and Gilbert, 2013; Rojas-Duran and Gilbert, 2012; Malabat et al., 2015; Sample et al., 2019; Cuperus et al., 2017; Akirtava and McManus, 2021; Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: TSS selection by S. cerevisiae Pol II occurs over a range of positions located ~40–120 bp downstream of the core promoter region.
source: TSS selection by S. cerevisiae Pol II occurs over a range of positions located ~40–120 bp downstream of the core promoter region.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of yeast TSS selection.

claim: Numerous lines of evidence suggest that TSS selection by S. cerevisiae Pol II involves a unidirectional scanning mechanism in which the preinitiation complex (PIC) assembles at an upstream core promoter and interrogates consecutive downstream positions for usable TSSs.
source: Numerous lines of evidence suggest that TSS selection by S. cerevisiae Pol II involves a unidirectional scanning mechanism in which the preinitiation complex (PIC) assembles at an upstream core promoter and interrogates consecutive downstream positions for usable TSSs (Giardina and Lis, 1993; Kuehner and Brow, 2006; Hampsey, 2006; Fishburn et al., 2016; Qiu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing the scanning model.

claim: TFIIH is proposed to drive Pol II scanning through ATP-dependent DNA translocase activity.
source: TFIIH is proposed to drive Pol II scanning through ATP-dependent DNA translocase activity (Fishburn et al., 2016; Tomko et al., 2021; Tomko et al., 2017; Fishburn et al., 2015; Fazal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposal supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: An optical-tweezer-based single molecule analysis of reconstituted S. cerevisiae PICs indicated that an ATP/dATP-induced activity within the PIC causes shortening of the distance between upstream and downstream DNA.
source: An optical-tweezer-based single molecule analysis of reconstituted S. cerevisiae PICs indicated that an ATP/dATP-induced activity within the PIC causes shortening of the distance between upstream and downstream DNA (Fazal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: This shortened distance approximates the distance downstream from TATA elements where TSSs are positioned in yeast (40–120 nt).
source: This shortened distance approximates the distance downstream from TATA elements where TSSs are positioned in yeast (40–120 nt) (Struhl, 1987)
evidence: This is an observation connecting optical tweezer data to known TSS positions, supported by citation.

claim: A magnetic tweezer-based single molecule assay suggested that an initial melted region of 6 nt (a 'bubble') is the direct consequence of TFIIH's ATPase activity.
source: Separately, a magnetic tweezer-based single molecule assay suggested that an initial melted region of 6 nt (a 'bubble') is the direct consequence of TFIIH's ATPase activity (Tomko et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: An ATP-dependent PIC activity for promoter opening is likely Ssl2 within TFIIH, which has been demonstrated as a DNA translocase within purified TFIIH in vitro.
source: Nevertheless, both studies agree that an ATP-dependent PIC activity for promoter opening is likely Ssl2 within TFIIH, which has been demonstrated as a DNA translocase within purified TFIIH in vitro (Fishburn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior biochemical work.

claim: ssl2 mutants have been identified as altering TSS selection at ADH1 and showed genetic interactions with sua7 (TFIIB) mutants.
source: In support of Ssl2/TFIIH's role in movement of downstream DNA toward the PIC, ssl2 mutants have been identified as altering TSS selection at ADH1 and showed genetic interactions with sua7 (TFIIB) mutants (Goel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited prior study.

claim: The identified ssl2 mutants shifted TSSs upstream at ADH1.
source: Specifically, the identified ssl2 mutants shifted TSSs upstream at ADH1.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited prior study.

claim: Polar shifts in TSSs distributions have been observed in mutants within Pol II, the GTFs TFIIB and TFIIF, and the PIC cofactor Sub1.
source: Polar shifts in TSSs distributions have been observed in mutants within Pol II, the GTFs TFIIB and TFIIF, and the PIC cofactor Sub1 (Kuehner and Brow, 2006; Qiu et al., 2020; Goel et al., 2012; Yang and Ponticelli, 2012; Khaperskyy et al., 2008; Pal et al., 2005; Majovski et al., 2005; Freire-Picos et al., 2005; Ghazy et al., 2004; Chen and Hampsey, 2004; Faitar et al., 2001; Pappas and Hampsey, 2000; Wu et al., 1999; Bangur et al., 1999; Pardee et al., 1998; Sun et al., 1996; Sun and Hampsey, 1995; Pinto et al., 1994; Berroteran et al., 1994; Pinto et al., 1992; Hampsey et al., 1991; Knaus et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior work.

claim: Polar (directional) shifts were observed at essentially all promoters examined across the genome in yeast for tested Pol II and GTF mutants, as predicted for scanning operating universally across promoter classes.
source: We have recently observed polar (directional) shifts at essentially all promoters examined across the genome in yeast for tested Pol II and GTF mutants, as predicted for scanning operating universally across promoter classes (Qiu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors.

claim: Hyperactive Pol II catalytic mutants shifted TSSs' distributions upstream at promoters genome-wide, consistent with a higher probability of initiation at every TSS.
source: We found that hyperactive Pol II catalytic mutants shifted TSSs' distributions upstream at promoters genome-wide, consistent with a higher probability of initiation at every TSS, and thus, initiation happening on average earlier in the scanning process.
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors with mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Hypoactive Pol II catalytic mutants shift TSS distributions downstream at promoters genome-wide, consistent with initiation happening later in the scanning process.
source: Conversely, hypoactive Pol II catalytic mutants shift TSS distributions downstream at promoters genome-wide, consistent with initiation happening later in the scanning process.
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors with mechanistic interpretation.

claim: Genetic interactions between Pol II and TFIIF or TFIIB support the idea that these mutations altered initiation additively, consistent with their acting in the same pathway during scanning.
source: Our previous data on genetic interactions between Pol II and TFIIF or TFIIB support the idea that these mutations altered initiation additively (Jin and Kaplan, 2014), consistent with their acting in the same pathway during scanning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of genetic interaction data from a prior study by the authors.

claim: Tested TFIIB mutants appeared to reduce initiation efficiency while tested TFIIF mutants appeared to increase initiation efficiency.
source: Tested TFIIB mutants appeared to reduce initiation efficiency while tested TFIIF mutants appeared to increase initiation efficiency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior experimental data.

claim: A double mutant between TFIIF and a hyperactive Pol II mutant had stronger effects on TSS shifts than either mutant alone across all promoters.
source: Consistent with this idea, a double mutant between TFIIF and a hyperactive Pol II mutant had stronger effects on TSS shifts than either mutant alone across all promoters.
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors.

claim: Pol II mutants are proposed to control initiation efficiency because active site residues important for catalytic activity alter TSS distributions correlating with the strengths of their catalytic defects in RNA chain elongation.
source: Pol II mutants are proposed to control initiation efficiency because active site residues important for catalytic activity alter TSS distributions correlating with the strengths of their catalytic defects in RNA chain elongation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on correlation between catalytic activity and TSS shifts.

claim: Initiation by promoter scanning should be dependent both on Pol II catalytic rate together and by whichever factors control the actual scanning step, that is, presumptively the rate and processivity of TFIIH as the putative scanning translocase.
source: Initiation by promoter scanning should be dependent both on Pol II catalytic rate together and by whichever factors control the actual scanning step, that is, presumptively the rate and processivity of TFIIH as the putative scanning translocase.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the scanning model.

claim: ssl2-DEAD and ssl2-508 exhibited strong and weak MPAS phenotypes, respectively.
source: Analysis of these five ssl2 mutants showed phenotypes consistent with altered TSS selection (Figure 1C). First, ssl2-DEAD and ssl2-508 exhibited strong and weak MPAS phenotypes, respectively.
evidence: This is directly observed in the phenotyping assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SSL2-1 exhibited a His+ phenotype, which is predictive of downstream shifts in TSS usage.
source: SSL2-1 exhibited a His+ phenotype, which is predictive of downstream shifts in TSS usage and consistent with its identification as a dominant mutant bypassing an inhibitory stem loop in the his4-316 mRNA (Gulyas and Donahue, 1992).
evidence: This is observed in phenotyping assays and connected to prior characterization.

claim: ssl2-rtt and rad25-ts24 show temperature-sensitive phenotypes.
source: ssl2-rtt and rad25-ts24 show temperature-sensitive phenotypes as expected; however, assayed transcription-related plate phenotypes were not observed.
evidence: This is observed in phenotyping assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no lys2-128∂ Spt- phenotype observed among these five existing ssl2 alleles.
source: Notably, there was no lys2-128∂ Spt- phenotype observed among these five existing ssl2 alleles, in contrast to our previous observation of an Spt- phenotype in a subset of MPAS Pol II TSS alleles (Kaplan et al., 2008; Braberg et al., 2013)
evidence: This is observed in phenotyping assays and compared to prior observations.

claim: ssl2-DEAD and ssl2-508 showed upstream shifts in their ADH1 TSS distributions.
source: As predicted from plate phenotypes observed and a previous study (Goel et al., 2012), ssl2-DEAD and ssl2-508 showed upstream shifts in their ADH1 TSS distributions (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This is shown by primer extension data in Figure 1E.

claim: ssl2-DEAD and ssl2-508 appeared primarily to reduce downstream TSS usage (loss in bin 5 and gain in bin 3).
source: However, we observed that these ssl2 alleles were quantitatively distinct in the amount of upstream shifting from Pol II and GTF alleles with comparable MPA sensitivities. ssl2-DEAD and ssl2-508 appeared primarily to reduce downstream TSS usage (loss in bin 5 and gain in bin 3)
evidence: This is observed in the quantification of primer extension data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The His+ SSL2-1 mutant shifted the overall TSS distribution downstream through increased relative downstream TSS utilization.
source: Consistent with the prediction based on its imd2Δ::HIS3 phenotype, the His+ SSL2-1 mutant shifted the overall TSS distribution downstream through increased relative downstream TSS utilization (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This is shown by primer extension data in Figure 1E.

claim: ssl2-rtt and rad25-ts24 had no obvious effects on TSS utilization at ADH1.
source: Two other mutants, ssl2-rtt and rad25-ts24, had no obvious effects on TSS utilization at ADH1, consistent with their lack of plate phenotypes (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This is shown by primer extension data in Figure 1E.

claim: Q592*, which creates a C-terminally truncated Ssl2 protein, confers lethality.
source: Of these, Q592*, which creates a C-terminally truncated Ssl2 protein (Oh et al., 2006), confers lethality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is observed in viability assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: T176P confers little if any growth defects and no MPAS or His+ phenotypes.
source: T176P (Cleaver et al., 1999; Weeda et al., 1997; Weeda et al., 1991) confers little if any growth defects and no MPAS or His+ phenotypes (Figure 1F), consistent with unaltered TSS usage (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is observed in phenotyping assays shown in Figure 1F and primer extension in Figure 1G.

claim: F156S conferred a mild MPAS phenotype and shifted TSS distribution upstream at ADH1.
source: In contrast, F156S (Cleaver et al., 1999; Weeda et al., 1991; Vermeulen et al., 1994) conferred a mild MPAS phenotype and shifted TSS distribution upstream at ADH1 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is observed in phenotyping and primer extension data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Y750* shows a mild to moderate level MPAS phenotype and shifts TSS distribution upstream at ADH1.
source: Mutant Y750*, which mimics a disease-related C-terminally truncated protein (Goel et al., 2012; Sweder and Hanawalt, 1994; Weeda et al., 1990), shows a mild to moderate level MPAS phenotype (Figure 1F) and shifts TSS distribution upstream at ADH1 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is observed in phenotyping and primer extension data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: RED motif substitutions in ssl2 confer lethal phenotypes.
source: The lethal phenotypes of RED motif substitutions in ssl2 revealed their essential roles in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is observed in viability assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A subset of human disease alleles can alter TFIIH functions when placed in the yeast system.
source: These results suggest that a subset of human disease alleles can alter TFIIH functions when placed in the yeast system.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some human disease alleles show phenotypes in yeast.

claim: All tested MPAS alleles shifted TSS usage upstream and all His+ alleles shifted TSS usage downstream.
source: We find that the two major classes of ssl2 mutants exhibited predicted TSS shifts, with all tested MPAS alleles shifting TSS usage upstream and all His+ alleles shifting TSS usage downstream (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is shown by primer extension data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Substitutions causing MPAS phenotypes and upstream TSS shifts alter amino acids distributed across the protein, with a large number in conserved domains and highly conserved residues.
source: Substitutions causing MPAS phenotypes and upstream TSS shifts alter amino acids distributed across the protein, with a large number in conserved domains and highly conserved residues (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by mapping mutations onto the Ssl2 structure and sequence alignment in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mutations related to His+ phenotypes, while also generally conserved, alter amino acids clustered N-terminally, within a domain predicted and now observed to be homologous to Ssl2's interaction partner Tfb2.
source: In contrast, mutations related to His+ phenotypes, while also generally conserved, alter amino acids clustered N-terminally, within a domain predicted (Luo et al., 2015; He et al., 2016) and now observed to be homologous to Ssl2's interaction partner Tfb2 (Schilbach et al., 2021; Greber et al., 2019; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by mapping mutations onto the Ssl2 structure in Figure 2A and supported by citations.

claim: The Spt- phenotype was found exclusively within a subset of stronger downstream TSS shifting His+ mutants.
source: In addition, the Spt- phenotype, not previously observed for classical ssl2 alleles, was found exclusively within a subset of stronger downstream TSS shifting His+ mutants (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in phenotyping data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Pol II mutants, the Spt- phenotype was observed in Pol II catalytic center substitutions, overlapping with MPAS to a large extent, and tightly linked with increased Pol II activity.
source: In our previous studies of Pol II mutants, the Spt- phenotype was observed in Pol II catalytic center substitutions, overlapping with MPAS to a large extent, and tightly linked with increased Pol II activity (Kaplan et al., 2012; Kaplan et al., 2008; Braberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from prior studies by the authors.

claim: In identified ssl2 alleles, none of the Spt- mutants also conferred MPAS.
source: However, in our identified ssl2 alleles, none of the Spt- mutants also conferred MPAS (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in phenotyping data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Some TSS shifting substitutions are located on the Ssl2 surface.
source: Some TSS shifting substitutions are located on the Ssl2 surface (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is shown by mapping mutations onto the Ssl2 structure in Figure 2B.

claim: D610A confers an upstream TSS shift.
source: D610A confers an upstream TSS shift.
evidence: This is observed in TSS analysis data.

claim: R636C confers a downstream TSS shift.
source: In contrast, R636C, which is also close to DNA, confers a downstream TSS shift.
evidence: This is observed in TSS analysis data.

claim: F498L caused an upstream TSS shift.
source: F498, which is located in the groove of Ssl2 lobe 1 and facing DNA, caused an upstream TSS shift when substituted with leucine.
evidence: This is observed in TSS analysis data.

claim: Substitutions D522V, K523N, N528I, F529L, and E537G shift TSSs upstream.
source: These substitutions are from the helicase domain 1 and shift TSSs upstream, including D522V, K523N, N528I, F529L, and E537G.
evidence: This is observed in TSS analysis data.

claim: Substitutions I383T and K372E shift TSS downstream.
source: In addition, substitutions I383T and K372E are in residues proximal to this small patch but shift TSS downstream.
evidence: This is observed in TSS analysis data.

claim: N230D/S confers MPAS and upstream TSS shifts, while N230I confers both His+ and Spt- phenotypes and a downstream TSS shift.
source: Highlighting the uniqueness and potential plasticity of this region, we identified multiple substitutions at the conserved N230 in this domain, with N230D/S conferring MPAS and an upstream TSS shifts, while N230I conferred both His+ and Spt- phenotypes and a downstream TSS shift (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is observed in phenotyping and TSS analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: ssl2 N230D is MPA sensitive and appears to reduce ability to use downstream TSSs at ADH1.
source: We highlight two alleles as representative of distinct ssl2 allele classes in comparison to examples of the two Pol II allele classes: ssl2 N230D, which is MPA sensitive and appears to reduce ability to use downstream TSSs at ADH1
evidence: This is shown in phenotyping and primer extension data in Figure 2G and H.

claim: ssl2 N230I shows both His+ and Spt- phenotypes and shifts TSSs downstream relative to WT at ADH1.
source: ssl2 N230I, which shows both His+ and Spt- phenotypes and shifts TSSs downstream relative to WT at ADH1 (Figure 2E and F rpb1 alleles, 2G and H ssl2 alleles).
evidence: This is shown in phenotyping and primer extension data in Figure 2G and H.

claim: rpb1 E1103G is MPAS and shifts TSS usage upstream.
source: As a comparison, rpb1 E1103G is MPAS and shifts TSS usage upstream
evidence: This is shown in phenotyping and primer extension data in Figure 2E and F.

claim: rpb1 H1085Y is His+ and shifts TSS usage downstream.
source: rpb1 H1085Y is His+ and shifts TSS usage downstream (Malik et al., 2017; Kaplan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in phenotyping and primer extension data in Figure 2E and F, and supported by citations.

claim: All ssl2 MPAS alleles examined appear to shift TSS distribution upstream by limiting or truncating TSS usage at downstream sites and not by activating lowly used upstream sites as rpb1 E1103G does.
source: However, all ssl2 MPAS alleles examined appear to shift TSS distribution upstream by limiting or truncating TSS usage at downstream sites and not by activating lowly used upstream sites as rpb1 E1103G does (and as known TFIIF alleles do) (Fishburn et al., 2015; Figure 2F and H).
evidence: This is observed by comparing primer extension patterns in Figure 2F and H.

claim: rpb1 and ssl2 alleles may alter TSS usage by distinct mechanisms.
source: This behavior suggests that rpb1 and ssl2 alleles may alter TSS usage by distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct patterns of TSS shifts observed.

claim: Clustering of correlation coefficients among libraries could distinguish Pol II mutants into GOF and LOF groups.
source: We previously found that clustering of correlation coefficients among libraries could distinguish Pol II mutants into GOF and LOF groups (Qiu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors.

claim: Mutant phenotypic classes were distinguished by clustering with ssl2 and Pol II alleles separated.
source: Here, we also found that mutant phenotypic classes were distinguished by this clustering with ssl2 and Pol II alleles separated suggesting effects observed at individual promoters are predictive of effects observed across the genome (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by hierarchical clustering analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: ssl2 alleles shift TSS distribution genome-wide.
source: ssl2 alleles shift TSS distribution genome-wide.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by TSS-seq data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Decreased TSS signal downstream of the WT median TSS signal was observed in ssl2 N230D and other ssl2 MPAS alleles.
source: We observed decreased TSS signal downstream of the WT median TSS signal in ssl2 N230D and other ssl2 MPAS alleles (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in heatmaps in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substantially increased TSS usage was observed at downstream sites in ssl2 N230I and other ssl2 His+ alleles.
source: In contrast, substantially increased TSS usage was observed at downstream sites in ssl2 N230I and other ssl2 His+ alleles (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in heatmaps in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ssl2 MPAS alleles shift the median TSS positions upstream at most promoters, showing a similar profile to Pol II GOF mutant.
source: As predicted from our model, ssl2 MPAS alleles shift the median TSS positions upstream at most promoters, showing a similar profile to Pol II GOF mutant (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in heatmaps and boxplots in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ssl2 His+ alleles shift median TSS positions downstream at the majority of promoters and show a similar profile to a Pol II LOF mutant.
source: Also as predicted from our model, ssl2 His+ alleles shift median TSS positions downstream at the majority of promoters and show a similar profile to a Pol II LOF mutant (Qiu et al., 2020; Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in heatmaps and boxplots in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mutants were clustered into upstream and downstream classes based on shifts in promoter median TSS position.
source: Additionally, mutants were clustered into upstream and downstream classes based on shifts in promoter median TSS position (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown by hierarchical clustering in Figure 4D.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) of TSS shifts distinguishes ssl2 and Pol II mutants into four major classes.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of TSS shifts distinguishes ssl2 and Pol II mutants into four major classes, namely Pol II LOF (downstream shifting) and GOF (upstream shifting), and ssl2 upstream and downstream shifting mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown by PCA analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The magnitude of TSS shift was consistent with the strengths of putative TSS shift-dependent growth phenotypes in ssl2 upstream shifting mutants.
source: We observed that the magnitude of TSS shift was consistent with the strengths of putative TSS shift-dependent growth phenotypes in ssl2 upstream shifting mutants (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown by comparing phenotype strengths to TSS shift magnitudes in Figure 4E.

claim: The extents of TSS shifts in ssl2 alleles are less than for Pol II activity mutants.
source: Notably, the extents of TSS shifts in ssl2 alleles are less than for Pol II activity mutants, indicating a more dramatic effect of Pol II's catalytic activity on TSS distributions (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown by comparing TSS shift magnitudes in Figure 4E.

claim: Obvious narrowing of TSS spreads was observed in ssl2 upstream shifting mutants and widening of TSS spreads in ssl2 downstream shifting mutants.
source: We observed obvious narrowing of TSS spreads in ssl2 upstream shifting mutants and widening of TSS spreads in ssl2 downstream shifting mutants (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is shown in boxplots and heatmaps in Figure 5B-D.

claim: MPAS ssl2 alleles showed narrowing in TSS spread at the majority of promoters while His+ ssl2 alleles showed widening in TSS spread at the majority of promoters.
source: Consistently, MPAS ssl2 alleles (those that shift TSSs upstream) showed narrowing in TSS spread at the majority of promoters while His+ ssl2 alleles (those that shift TSSs downstream) showed widening in TSS spread at the majority of promoters.
evidence: This is shown in TSS spread analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Classes of initiation allele may be easily identified for Pol II or SSL2 using the same genetic phenotypes, but their effects on TSSs at individual promoters are quantitatively and likely qualitatively distinct.
source: These results extend the idea that while classes of initiation allele may be easily identified for Pol II or SSL2 using the same genetic phenotypes, their effects on TSSs at individual promoters are quantitatively and likely qualitatively distinct.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the distinct patterns of TSS shifts and spread changes between Pol II and ssl2 alleles.

claim: ssl2 alleles that narrow TSS spreads are defective in scanning processivity due to decreased Ssl2/TFIIH translocase activity.
source: To explain the observed quantitative differences between Pol II initiation efficiency alleles and ssl2 alleles, we hypothesize that ssl2 alleles that narrow TSS spreads (ssl2 N230D and similar alleles), resulting in upstream shifts in TSS distributions, are defective in scanning processivity due to decreased Ssl2/TFIIH translocase activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed data.

claim: ssl2 alleles that show increased TSS spreads and usage at downstream sites behave as increased scanning processivity (GOF) alleles, due to an increase in Ssl2/TFIIH activity.
source: In contrast, ssl2 alleles that show increased TSS spreads and usage at downstream sites (N230I and similar alleles) behave as increased scanning processivity (GOF) alleles, due to an increase in Ssl2/TFIIH activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed data.

claim: Pol II activity mutants and alleles of GTFs (sua7/TFIIB and tfg2/TFIIF) showed additivity/suppression for transcription-dependent phenotypes as well as additivity/suppression for alterations to TSS distributions at ADH1.
source: In our previous studies, we found that Pol II activity mutants and alleles of GTFs (sua7/TFIIB and tfg2/TFIIF) showed additivity/suppression for transcription-dependent phenotypes as well as additivity/suppression for alterations to TSS distributions at ADH1.
evidence: This is a finding from prior studies by the authors.

claim: Primarily epistatic effects were observed between Pol II and ssl2 alleles.
source: In contrast to the suppressive/additive interactions that were broadly observed between Pol II and TFIIB/TFIIF alleles (Jin and Kaplan, 2014), we observe primarily epistatic effects between Pol II and ssl2 alleles.
evidence: This is a primary finding from genetic interaction studies shown in Figure 6.

claim: Nearly complete absence of synthetic lethality was observed between ssl2 downstream shifting alleles and Pol II downstream shifting alleles.
source: This epistasis is best reflected by nearly complete absence of synthetic lethality between ssl2 downstream shifting alleles and Pol II downstream shifting alleles (Figure 6A–C)
evidence: This is shown in genetic interaction data in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Epistasis for both transcription phenotypes and ADH1 TSS shifts was observed between Pol II upstream shifting alleles and both classes of ssl2 allele.
source: Epistasis for both transcription phenotypes and ADH1 TSS shifts was also observed between Pol II upstream shifting alleles and both classes of ssl2 allele, meaning that double mutants had phenotypes of Pol II single mutants (Figure 6A–K, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in genetic interaction data in Figure 6.

claim: Both classes of ssl2 alleles appeared epistatic or non-additive with Pol II downstream shifting alleles.
source: Similarly, both classes of ssl2 alleles appeared epistatic or non-additive with Pol II downstream shifting alleles (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is shown in genetic interaction data in Figure 6.

claim: Lethal phenotypes were observed between individual ssl2 alleles and sua7-1 or tfg2∆146–180 alleles for combinations between single mutants that alter TSS distributions in the same direction.
source: Notably, lethal phenotypes were observed between individual ssl2 alleles and sua7-1 or tfg2∆146–180 alleles for combinations between single mutants that alter TSS distributions in the same direction, distinct from their interactions with Pol II alleles (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in genetic interaction data in Figure 7A.

claim: When alleles of sua7-1 or tfg2∆146–180 were combined with ssl2 alleles that shift TSS distributions in opposite directions, interactions were complex but significant epistasis was observed.
source: When we combined alleles of sua7-1 or tfg2∆146–180 with ssl2 alleles that shift TSS distributions in opposite directions, interactions were complex but significant epistasis was observed.
evidence: This is shown in genetic interaction data in Figure 7.

claim: Double mutants between sua7-1 or tfg2∆146–180 and ssl2 alleles shifted ADH1 TSS distributions to similar extent as the tfg2∆146–180 single mutant.
source: Consistently, double mutants shifted ADH1 TSS distributions to similar extent as the tfg2∆146–180 single mutant (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is shown in primer extension data in Figure 7C.

claim: sub1∆ confers a His+ phenotype for the imd2Δ::HIS3 initiation reporter.
source: We previously found sub1∆ to confer a His+ phenotype for the imd2Δ::HIS3 initiation reporter (Malik et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors.

claim: Pol II GOF alleles appeared epistatic to sub1∆.
source: furthermore found that Pol II GOF alleles appeared epistatic to sub1∆, leading to the proposal that sub1∆ effects in initiation were distinct from TFIIB or TFIIF alleles (Jin and Kaplan, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors.

claim: No strong genetic interactions (lethality) were observed between ssl2 and sub1Δ alleles, save for one specific case.
source: First, no strong genetic interactions (lethality) were observed between ssl2 and sub1Δ alleles, save for one specific case (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in genetic interaction data in Figure 7A.

claim: The majority of sub1∆ interactions with ssl2 alleles appear to be additive when examining TSS distributions at ADH1.
source: Second, the majority of sub1∆ interactions with ssl2 alleles appear to be additive when examining TSS distributions at ADH1 as predicted for factors are acting on processivity independently.
evidence: This is shown in primer extension data in Figure 7D.

claim: Most upstream shifting ssl2 alleles were additive with sub1∆ for TSS distributions at ADH1, resulting in mutual suppression of TSS distribution shifts.
source: For example, most upstream shifting ssl2 alleles were additive with sub1∆ for TSS distributions at ADH1, resulting in mutual suppression of TSS distribution shifts (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in primer extension data in Figure 7D.

claim: sub1∆ was epistatic to ssl2 Y750*.
source: In contrast, sub1∆ was epistatic to ssl2 Y750*, suggesting that a putative block to processivity due to C-terminal truncation of Ssl2 can be relieved by sub1∆, and potentially may be due to altered Sub1 function in ssl2 Y750*.
evidence: This is shown in genetic interaction data in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: ssl2 F498L was unexpectedly synthetic lethal with both sua7-1 and sub1∆.
source: Finally, allele specificity of ssl2 F498L was revealed by these genetic experiments. This TSS upstream shifting ssl2 allele was unexpectedly synthetic lethal with both sua7-1 and sub1∆ suggesting heretofore undetected phenotypic differences from other alleles of the same class.
evidence: This is shown in genetic interaction data in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Results of genetic interaction studies are consistent with two distinct networks controlling TSS selection by scanning.
source: Results of genetic interaction studies are consistent with two distinct networks controlling TSS selection by scanning (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the integration of genetic interaction data.

claim: One network impinges on Pol II catalysis and initiation efficiency, and genetic analyses suggest that the Pol II active site collaborates with activities of TFIIB and TFIIH in this process.
source: One network impinges on Pol II catalysis and initiation efficiency, and genetic analyses suggest that the Pol II active site collaborates with activities of TFIIB and TFIIH in this process, consistent with experiments indicating effects of TFIIB and TFIIF on Pol II catalytic activity (e.g., Khaperskyy et al., 2008; Cabart et al., 2014; Sainsbury et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on genetic interaction data and supported by citations.

claim: The other network appears to alter TSS distributions through regulating TFIIH's processivity, and includes Ssl2, Sub1, and potentially TFIIF.
source: The other, we propose, impinges on scanning processivity through TFIIH with the participation of Sub1.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on genetic interaction data.

claim: Both ssl2 N230D and ssl2 N230I shifted PIC localization genome-wide with the same polarity as they shift TSS distributions.
source: We performed these same ChIP-exo experiments on Sua7 and Ssl2 for two ssl2 alleles, N230D and N230I (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, B). Both shifted PIC localization genome-wide with the same polarity as they shift TSS distributions.
evidence: This is shown in ChIP-exo data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The extent of ChIP-exo shifts were as strong or stronger than Pol II mutant shifts although Pol II mutants have stronger effects on TSS distributions.
source: The extent of ChIP-exo shifts were as strong or stronger than Pol II mutant shifts although Pol II mutants have stronger effects on TSS distributions (Qiu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is observed by comparing ChIP-exo data to prior Pol II mutant data.

claim: Our studies reveal the impact of altered Ssl2 function on initiation by promoter scanning in S. cerevisiae.
source: Our studies now reveal the impact of altered Ssl2 function on initiation by promoter scanning in S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Distinct classes of Ssl2 allele alter initiation genome-wide with distinct behaviors, with many alleles being in highly conserved residues.
source: We find distinct classes of Ssl2 allele that alter initiation genome-wide with distinct behaviors, with many alleles being in highly conserved residues.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Genomic and genetic data support a model wherein Ssl2 function as a DNA translocase can be genetically modulated and this modulation is consistent with TFIIH having either increased or decreased processivity during promoter scanning.
source: Our genomic and genetic data support a model wherein Ssl2 function as a DNA translocase can be genetically modulated and this modulation is consistent with TFIIH having either increased or decreased processivity during promoter scanning.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the integration of all experimental findings.

claim: One class of ssl2 alleles behaves biochemically as an LOF and therefore truncates the scanning process prematurely and narrows TSS distributions genome-wide.
source: The positioning and genetic behaviors of our allele classes are consistent with one class behaving biochemically as an LOF and therefore truncating the scanning process prematurely and narrowing TSS distributions genome-wide.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data consistent with decreased translocase processivity.

claim: Another class of ssl2 alleles increases downstream TSS usage and alters PIC localization at promoters by extending it downstream, consistent with increased translocase processivity.
source: Conversely, our other class increases downstream TSS usage and alters PIC localization at promoters by extending it downstream. These behaviors are consistent with increased translocase processivity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data consistent with increased translocase processivity.

claim: Putative increased SSL2 activity alleles are also dominant or codominant genetically.
source: Putative increased SSL2 activity alleles are also dominant or codominant genetically, consistent with being able to function on promoters in an increased capacity of some sort.
evidence: This is observed in genetic dominance tests.
